comments.value: The windbg-eac-full is the windbg transcript.

details:
SUMMARY

The Easy Anti-Cheat EOS kernel driver (EasyAntiCheat_EOS.sys) fails to unload after VRChat exits. The Windows service EasyAntiCheat_EOSSys remains in STOP_PENDING, potentially preventing subsequent game launches until the machine is restarted.

I investigated this issue using WinDbg and a Full Live Kernel Memory Dump.

The dump shows that an EAC-related system worker thread is blocked inside nt!CmUnRegisterCallback, waiting for an EAC registry callback record to become eligible for removal.

The callback record's state field contains 0x80000001, while the unregister routine is waiting for 0x80000000. Based on the disassembly, this strongly suggests that one outstanding callback reference is preventing the registry callback from being unregistered.

The exact owner or source of that outstanding reference has not yet been identified.

ENVIRONMENT

Operating system: Windows 11, build 26200 (exact revision not confirmed)

Game: VRChat (Steam / PC)

Affected service: EasyAntiCheat_EOSSys

Driver: EasyAntiCheat_EOS.sys

Driver file version: 3.2.0.0

Driver timestamp: September 8, 2026, 16:47:40

Driver image size: 0x02AB9000

Debugging tools: WinDbg, Microsoft kernel symbols, Full Live Kernel Memory Dump

VRChat version: 1920

OBSERVED BEHAVIOR

VRChat can initially be launched and used normally.

After VRChat exits, the EAC kernel driver does not unload as expected.

The EasyAntiCheat_EOSSys service remains in or enters STOP_PENDING when a stop is requested.

The EAC kernel driver remains loaded, and restarting VRChat may fail until the machine is rebooted.

Kernel debugging shows that the driver is blocked during registry callback unregistration.

Expected behavior: EAC should complete its shutdown and unload its kernel driver when it is no longer required by VRChat.

Actual behavior: The EAC shutdown path remains blocked indefinitely, leaving the driver loaded.

The precise trigger is not yet known, and I do not currently have reliable minimal reproduction steps.

WINDbg INVESTIGATION

SECTION 1 — BLOCKED THREAD

The affected thread is a system worker thread.

ETHREAD: ffffd70065491040

Process: System (PID 4)

TID: 0x970c

State: WAIT (WrPushLock)

Mode: KernelMode Non-Alertable

Relevant call stack, from the waiting function towards its caller:

nt!KiSwapContext

nt!KiSwapThread

nt!KiCommitThreadWait

nt!KeWaitForSingleObject

nt!ExTimedWaitForUnblockPushLock+0xc9

nt!ExBlockOnAddressPushLock+0x98

nt!CmUnRegisterCallback+0xc4

EasyAntiCheat_EOS+0x3cb6b2

WinDbg reported the following wait duration:

Ticks: 7598937 (1:08:58:53.390)

This corresponds to approximately 32 hours and 59 minutes of waiting in the captured snapshot.

SECTION 2 — REGISTRY CALLBACK RECORD

Using the saved context of the CmUnRegisterCallback stack frame, I recovered the following register values:

Command: .frame /c /r 6

RSI = 0000000080000000

RDI = ffff910ade2d6440

RIP = fffff8017addf364

The callback record's state field was read directly from the full kernel dump.

Command: dd @rdi+0x10 L1

Address: ffff910a`de2d6450

Value: 80000001

Disassembly of nt!CmUnRegisterCallback shows the following relevant operations:

lock or dword ptr [rdi+10h],80000000h

call nt!CmpUnlockCallbackList

mov esi,80000000h

call nt!ExBlockOnAddressPushLock

mov eax,dword ptr [rdi+10h]

cmp eax,esi

jne nt!CmUnRegisterCallback+0xa0

The routine sets the high bit of the callback record's state field and waits for that field to equal 0x80000000 before continuing with callback removal.

Interpretation:

The high bit appears to represent pending deletion, while the remaining bits appear to track active callback references.

The observed state of 0x80000001 is consistent with one remaining active reference.

This interpretation is based on the observed Windows kernel implementation, not a publicly documented structure layout.

SECTION 3 — POOL ALLOCATION AND CALLBACK OWNERSHIP

The callback record resides inside an allocated Configuration Manager pool object.

Command: !pool ffff910ade2d6440

Result:

Allocation address: ffff910ade2d6430

Allocation size: 0x60

Allocation status: Allocated

Pool tag: CMcb

Description: Internal Configuration manager allocations

Binary: nt!cm

Relevant callback record contents:

Address ffff910a`de2d6440: ffff910a`758e1e40

Address ffff910a`de2d6448: ffff910a`73e4ec20

Address ffff910a`de2d6450: 00000000`80000001

Address ffff910a`de2d6458: 01dd54bb`bbb42c58

Address ffff910a`de2d6460: 00000000`00000000

Address ffff910a`de2d6468: fffff801`2faffa7f

The value at offset +0x18 matches the registry callback cookie saved in RBX by CmUnRegisterCallback.

The value at offset +0x28 points into the EAC driver image:

fffff801`2faffa7f = EasyAntiCheat_EOS+0x22fa7f

This is consistent with an EAC-registered registry callback function pointer.

The callback record remains allocated in the captured dump.

SECTION 4 — ADDITIONAL EAC-ASSOCIATED THREADS

A system-wide stack search identified eight threads containing EAC code.

Six worker threads were blocked in a common EAC wait routine:

nt!KeWaitForSingleObject

EasyAntiCheat_EOS+0x3b3bc3

One additional thread was waiting in another EAC routine, and the eighth was the CmUnRegisterCallback thread described above.

These additional threads may be normal long-lived worker threads. Their presence alone does not establish a deadlock.

A search for nt!CmpCallCallBacksEx did not identify a matching active call stack among approximately 8,854 scanned threads.

This does not rule out an unfinished callback execution or a leaked callback reference.

SUSPECTED CAUSE

The strongest current hypothesis is that EAC's registry callback cannot be unregistered because an active callback reference remains outstanding indefinitely.

Potential explanations include a registry callback execution that never completes, a reference not being released on an error or cleanup path, an interaction with another kernel component, or a callback lifecycle synchronization defect during EAC shutdown.

The available evidence does not yet establish which explanation is correct.

Microsoft documents that calling CmUnRegisterCallback from within the registry callback itself causes deadlock.

However, the captured unregistering thread is a system worker thread, and there is currently no evidence that this specific documented misuse occurred.

Microsoft documentation:

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/ddi/wdm/nf-wdm-cmunregistercallback

RELATED PUBLIC REPORT

A previously tracked VRChat issue describes a similar EAC unload failure and STOP_PENDING state:

https://feedback.vrchat.com/bug-reports/p/eac-failing-to-unload-preventing-starting-vrchat-again

That report predates this investigation. Although the symptoms match closely, the available information does not establish that both incidents have the same root cause.

REQUEST TO DEVELOPERS

Could the VRChat team forward these findings to the Easy Anti-Cheat / Epic Games kernel driver development team?

I would particularly appreciate an investigation into the EAC registry callback at driver offset +0x22fa7f, the callback unregistration path near driver offset +0x3cb6b2, and the outstanding reference that appears to leave the callback record's state field at 0x80000001.

I would also appreciate a review of the error handling and synchronization logic involved in EAC driver shutdown.

The driver had already been blocked for an extended period when the full kernel dump was captured.

I can provide relevant WinDbg transcripts and additional debugging information.

A Full Live Kernel Memory Dump of approximately 4 GB is also available locally and could be shared privately upon request, subject to privacy and security considerations.

Thank you for investigating this issue.
title: Easy Anti-Cheat EOS driver stuck in STOP_PENDING — CmUnRegisterCallback waiting on outstanding registry callback reference
